# Write In Your Voice

For any person, any language. The output is a finished piece in their voice and format, plus an honest note of what it was built from.

## Reference Files

This file is the whole procedure. Open a reference file only when the piece needs it:

| The piece | Read |
|---|---|
| Reports of measurements, experiments, code runs or builds; anything with figures, tables or equations | `references/lab-and-technical-reports.md` |
| Papers, theses, reviews, or any text with a reference list | `references/papers-and-references.md` |
| Comparisons between conditions, measurement error, tests, conclusions drawn from numbers | `references/statistics-reporting.md` |

Scripts (run each with `--help` first):

- `scripts/docx_report_helpers.py`: python-docx layout helpers (page presets, titled tables, figures with outside captions, native or image equations).
- `scripts/verify_report_numbers.py`: recomputes the worked calculations stated in a finished report.

## 1. Settle Four Things Before Writing

1. **The piece.** Genre, reader, purpose, language, length.
2. **The rule of the context about AI.** This decides the mode.

   | Context | Mode |
   |---|---|
   | AI help allowed, or the person's own material with no rule (emails, notes, posts, internal documents) | Assisted drafting |
   | AI-written text not allowed (a course or exam that bans it, an application that requires the applicant's own writing) | Coach only (section 9) |
   | Graded or judged work with an unknown rule | Ask. Coach only until the rule is known |

   Do not help make AI-written text pass as someone's own where AI is not allowed. Add an AI-use statement when the context asks for one, and never write that a text was produced without AI help when it was not.
3. **The format.** Guideline, rubric, template, example documents, file type, page or word limit, required sections, citation style, file name. A supplied template is written in, not imitated. With no format given, use the convention of the genre and say which one was used.
4. **The material.** Their notes, data, results, code, sources, course material, earlier drafts.

Ask only what is needed to start. When working unattended, take the most reasonable reading and state it at the top of the result.

## 2. Voice Profile

Sources, strongest first:

1. Texts they wrote themselves in the same genre and language (two or three are enough).
2. A saved writing-style profile (a `my-voice.md` file in the workspace or attached to the request), or memory of how they write and what they have asked for before (tone, formatting, things to avoid).
3. Their messages in the current conversation. Weak evidence: chat register differs from formal writing.
4. Nothing available: write in a plain neutral style and say so.

What to take from the sources: sentence length and rhythm, person (I, we, impersonal), formality and sentence endings (in Korean, 합니다체 / 한다체 / 해요체), how much they hedge, the connectives they use, paragraph length, how they open and close, words they prefer or avoid, how they present numbers and citations, formatting habits.

Rules:

- For a long piece, state the profile in five to eight lines first and let them correct it.
- Imitate habits, not sentences. Do not paste their old sentences into the new text.
- Memory informs voice and preferences. Personal facts from memory go into the text only when they asked for that.
- Text written by other people or by AI is not evidence of their voice.
- Never say the voice was matched when no sample or profile was available.
- After building a profile from samples, offer to save it as `my-voice.md` so later requests, and agents without memory, can reuse it. Update that file when they correct the voice; do not rebuild it from scratch each time.

## 3. Evidence First

- Audit before drafting. List the statements the piece has to make and, for each, where it comes from: file, page, table cell, log value, code line. Open the real material (images, tables, code, slides) instead of relying on a description of it.
- Use what the audit surfaces: exact counts, names, dates, what a log shows over time, which function performs a step. These specifics are the substance of the text.
- Numbers come from the files. Build tables by script when possible and never retype figures from memory.
- Do not state what the material does not show. Say what was not done or not tested.

## 4. Drafting Rules

- Write what only this piece could say. Replace a general statement with the specific case.
- Attach a number, name, date or source to every claim that can carry one.
- First person for the person's own actions and judgments, and only when true. If the assistant did part of the work (ran an analysis, inspected files), tell them where and how, so the text describes the real process and they can confirm it.
- Short declarative sentences, one idea each. Hedge only real uncertainty.
- Avoid template patterns: First/Second/Third chains, mirrored sentence pairs, a summary line closing every paragraph, stock connectives in a row. When a fixed number of points is required, label them and give each a concrete case.
- Source and course material: cite the specific point (page, slide, section) and attach it to a fact of this piece in the same or the next sentence. Do not restate the source in bulk.
- An interpretation must match the numbers it rests on, including the categories it names. Check direction and labels against the table.
- Mark every part drafted without their notes, so they know what to review and reword.

## 5. Format Compliance

- Turn the guideline into a checklist: each required item, where it must appear, units and decimals, labels, limits, language, file type, file name.
- Produce the requested output type and use their template when one exists.
- Tables and figures follow the caption and title convention of their format, stay readable at the inserted size, and agree with the numbers in the text. Defaults when no template is given are in `references/lab-and-technical-reports.md`.
- Render the document and look at every page before delivery.

## 6. Verification Before Delivery

1. Every checklist item is present and in the right place.
2. Recompute each worked calculation from the text of the finished document. `scripts/verify_report_numbers.py report.pdf` does this for subtractions (`a - b = c`) and percentages (`100 x a / b = c %`); run it with `--help` first.
3. Compare tables with the source files.
4. Repeat the audit on the final text: each factual sentence has a source.
5. Quotations and references are checked against the originals. A reference that was not opened and checked does not go into the list (`references/papers-and-references.md`, section 3).
6. Files that had to stay unchanged are identical to the originals.

## 7. Revising

- Change one set of paragraphs at a time and confirm by diff that nothing else moved.
- Keep the previous version as a fallback.
- Rewording never changes facts, numbers or conclusions.

## 8. When An AI-Writing Check Report Is Provided (Assisted Drafting Only)

1. List the flagged blocks. Checkers merge headings, tables and captions into the block of a nearby paragraph, so map each block back to its paragraphs.
2. Flags concentrate in generic explanation: theory, lists of reasons, interpretation, restated source material. Rewrite only those paragraphs with sections 3 and 4. The person's own wording for the paragraph is the most effective source, so ask for it first.
3. Leave unflagged paragraphs alone unless a fact changes.
4. No tricks: no deliberate typos, odd characters, hidden text, synonym spinning or broken grammar. A revision that reads worse is not acceptable.
5. The checker cannot be run by the assistant. Never promise a percentage. The reported number is usually the share of text inside flagged blocks, and the checker may merge blocks differently on each run, so a rewrite that stays flagged can raise it.
6. Stop when the result is under the target the person named. Passages still flagged after two rounds should be written by the person.

What has worked: a general description replaced by a description of the actual inputs; a statement about method replaced by what the code does and when; one concrete case per reason, taken from the results; a plausible explanation backed by a logged value; a cited source point tied to a fact from the audit. Shortening or reordering sentences alone did not work.

## 9. Coach Only

The person writes every sentence. The assistant does not draft, rewrite, translate, paraphrase or polish their text, and does not supply sentences to copy. Follow the exact wording of the rule; if it also forbids AI feedback, stop and say so.

What the assistant does: turns the guideline into a checklist and reports what is covered and what is missing; asks what they want to claim, what evidence they have and who reads it; points to places in their draft and names the problem (claim without evidence, unclear referent, number that disagrees with a table, missing citation) so they can fix it; runs checks that produce no prose (arithmetic, units, numbering, reference format, limits, layout). Sections 3 to 6 serve as their self-check list. Code and data work follow the context's own rule for code, which may differ from its rule for prose.

Section 8 is not used in this mode.

## 10. Final Message

State the mode, the voice sources used (or that none were available), what was verified and how, what the person should confirm or reword themselves, and any known weakness of the piece.

# Lab, Experiment And Technical Reports

Read this when the piece reports measurements, experiments, code runs or a build. It adds layout and evidence rules to the main skill. The person's template or guideline always wins over the defaults here.

## 1. Map The Evidence First

- List every photo, screenshot, waveform, log and result file, and assign each to the experiment, condition and question it supports. Use the exact file names.
- Prefer original photos and screenshots over redrawn diagrams.
- A number that cannot be read with confidence from an image is marked for the person to confirm, or described qualitatively. Do not invent voltages, distances, error values or sample counts.
- Keep theory, measured result, comparison and discussion apart. Error and difference tables are computed from the stated values only.
- For a large job keep a short source list: which file fed which table or figure.

## 2. Reports Built From Code Outputs

- Generate the document with a build script that reads the result files (CSV, JSON, logs) directly. Do not retype numbers.
- Put assertions in the script that tie the prose to the data (which condition was largest, the sign of a difference, a count), so a rerun that changes a result stops the build instead of leaving stale text.
- Show worked calculations in a table column (`a - b`, result) or as an equation. State units and signs, and keep percent apart from percentage points.
- State the software versions and device that the run itself recorded.
- Say where the run happened. If the assistant ran it, the person must know, because the version table describes that run.
- Compare supplied files that had to stay unchanged byte for byte with the originals, and check each statement about a setting against the code that sets it.
- If only the report is graded, deliver the report and package code plus outputs separately, without large datasets or other bulky generated files.

## 3. Figures

- Centered image; the image area holds only the image or its panels.
- Caption in its own centered paragraph directly below the image, never inside the image box.
- Related panels may share one figure with one caption. Unrelated items get separate figures.
- Resolution: about 1800 px wide for a full-width figure, about 850 px for a half-width one, saved at 300 dpi or more. For crops from a PDF, render the page at 300-400 dpi first and crop that; do not enlarge a low-resolution crop.
- Plots made by code: choose the figure size so axis and legend text stay at about 7 pt or more at the inserted width. One colour per series across panels, a different marker shape per series, labelled axes with units, a legend.
- Insert at a fixed physical width so the page layout is stable.

## 4. Tables

- Title in its own centered paragraph directly above the table. Keep title and table on one page; move both to the next page if the title would be left behind.
- Compact grid, centered header row with light shading, readable cell padding. Long explanations belong in the prose, not in cells.
- Repeat the unit in the header. Use the number of decimals the guideline asks for, everywhere.

## 5. Equations

- Use the document's native equation objects (Office Math in DOCX, equation editor in HWP, math mode in LaTeX), not typed plain text.
- Center standalone equations and explain the variables in the sentence before or after.
- Split a long derivation over several lines.
- Converters without a formula renderer leave native equations blank (LibreOffice without its Math component does this). Keep native equations in the editable file and build a second copy for PDF export with the same equations typeset as 600 dpi images. Look at the rendered PDF to confirm.

## 6. Layout Presets

Use the person's template when there is one. Otherwise pick a preset and say which.

| Setting | Compact | Standard |
|---|---|---|
| Page | A4 | A4 |
| Margins (top / bottom / sides) | 2.2 / 2.0 / 2.3 cm | 2.5 / 2.5 / 2.5 cm |
| Body | 10 pt, line spacing 112%, left aligned | 11 pt, line spacing 150%, justified |
| Paragraph spacing | 5 pt before, 2.5 pt after | 0 before, 4 pt after |
| Figure caption | 9 pt bold, in brackets: `[Figure 2. ...]` | 9 pt, plain: `Figure 2. ...` |
| Table title | 9 pt bold, above: `Table 2. ...` | 9 pt, above: `Table 2. ...` |
| Table header fill | light blue `DDEBF7` | light gray `E7E7E7` |

Caption labels follow the language of the report (`그림 2.` / `표 2.` in Korean). Use the font the template names; when it is not installed, use the closest available face and tell the person.

`scripts/docx_report_helpers.py` applies these presets with python-docx: page setup, centered figure with outside caption, titled table, native equation, optional image equation.

## 7. Export

- DOCX to PDF: convert, then open the PDF and look at every page (blank equations, detached table titles, a figure pushed to the next page leaving half a page empty).
- HWP/HWPX: export through the Hancom application itself on the person's machine and reopen the result to check fonts and equations. The assistant cannot verify an HWP file it has not opened.
- Set the document author and title metadata to the person's, not to a tool default.

## 8. Final Checks For This Genre

1. Every figure and table is referred to in the text and numbered in order.
2. Every number in the prose matches its table; run `scripts/verify_report_numbers.py` on the finished file.
3. Axes, units, legends and any required markers are present on every plot.
4. The required items of the guideline sit under the question or section they belong to.

# Papers, Theses And Reference Lists

Read this when the piece is a paper, thesis chapter, review, or any text with a reference list.

## 1. Structure

Use the structure the venue or guideline prescribes. Without one, the usual order for an empirical paper is:

| Part | What it has to do |
|---|---|
| Title | Name the object and the finding or method, without filler words. |
| Abstract | Problem, what was done, the main result with its number, what follows. No citations, no undefined abbreviations. Write it last. |
| Introduction | The problem, what is known, the gap, what this work does. End with the contribution stated plainly. |
| Methods | Enough for someone else to repeat the work: data, procedure, settings, software versions, how results were evaluated. |
| Results | What was found, in the order of the questions asked. Numbers with units and uncertainty. No interpretation beyond what a reader needs to follow a table. |
| Discussion | What the results mean, how they compare with prior work, limitations, what was not tested. |
| Conclusion | The answer to the question in the introduction, limited to what the results support. |
| References | Every cited source, in the required style. |

Write body sections as paragraphs. Keep one claim per paragraph and put the evidence in the same paragraph.

## 2. Finding Sources

- Search with the tools the agent actually has (web search, a scholarly database connector, the person's reference manager). Say which were used.
- Prefer the original paper, standard or dataset page over a blog or summary. Prefer the published version over a preprint when both exist, and cite the one that was read.
- Search for sources that disagree with the claim as well as ones that support it.
- Stop when the claim is supported. A reference list is not a measure of effort.

## 3. Verifying Every Reference

No reference goes into the list unless all of this is true:

1. The source exists: the DOI resolves, or the publisher or archive page was opened.
2. Title, authors, year, venue, volume and pages were copied from that page, not from memory.
3. The source says what the sentence citing it says. Open it and find the passage; for a number, find the table.
4. The person can get to it: record the DOI or URL.

Never produce a reference from memory alone. A plausible citation that was not checked is treated as a fabricated one: leave the claim uncited and tell the person it needs a source.

Keep a small table while working: claim, source, where in the source (page, section, figure), verified yes or no.

## 4. Using Sources In The Text

- Cite the specific point and connect it to this work in the same or the next sentence. Do not summarize a source for a paragraph.
- Paraphrase by default. Quote only wording that matters as wording, keep quotations short, and mark them as quotations with the page.
- Separate what the source found from what this work concludes from it.
- Unpublished material (course notes, internal documents, talks) is cited as such, with its title, author or organization, and date.

## 5. Citation Styles

Use the style the venue names and apply it to every entry the same way.

| Style | In text | List order |
|---|---|---|
| IEEE | `[3]` | by first appearance |
| APA 7 | `(Kim & Lee, 2023)` | alphabetical by first author |
| Vancouver | `(3)` or superscript | by first appearance |
| Chicago author-date | `(Kim and Lee 2023)` | alphabetical |

With a reference manager or BibTeX, keep one entry per source, a stable key, and the DOI field filled. Check the rendered list: capitalization of titles, journal abbreviations, page ranges with an en dash, no "et al." where the style lists all authors.

## 6. Final Checks For This Genre

1. Every in-text citation has a list entry and every list entry is cited.
2. Numbering or ordering follows the style.
3. Every entry passed section 3.
4. Figures and tables taken from other work carry their source and any permission the venue requires.
5. The abstract's numbers match the results section.

# Reporting Experimental Statistics

Read this when the piece compares conditions, reports measurement error, or draws a conclusion from numbers. Compute with a script from the raw data and keep the script; do not do statistics in prose.

## 1. Before Any Test

- State the unit of analysis (image, subject, trial, run) and the count for each condition.
- State how the data were split or sampled, how many repetitions there were, and what was fixed.
- Decide the comparison before looking at the outcome when possible. If a comparison was chosen after seeing the data, say so.
- Look at the raw values or a plot first. A mean hides outliers, ceilings and bimodal results.

## 2. What To Report For Every Number

| Quantity | Report with it |
|---|---|
| Mean | standard deviation and n; a confidence interval when an inference is made |
| Median | interquartile range or min-max, and n |
| Proportion or rate | the counts behind it (k of n) and the size of one unit (one item out of 50 is 2 percentage points) |
| Difference between conditions | the two values, the signed difference, its unit, and an interval or a statement of what variation it should be compared with |
| Measured vs theoretical value | both values and the relative error, with the formula used |
| Fit | the model, the fitted parameters with units, and a goodness-of-fit measure |

Use percentage points for the difference between two percentages. Keep the sign of a difference. Use the number of decimals the guideline asks for; otherwise no more digits than the measurement supports.

## 3. Uncertainty With Small Samples

- For a proportion p measured on n items, the binomial standard error is sqrt(p(1-p)/n). With n = 100 and p = 0.5 it is 5 percentage points, so a difference of a few points between two such numbers is within noise.
- Two methods measured on the same items are paired. Compare them item by item (which items one got right and the other wrong), not as two independent proportions.
- A single run gives no estimate of run-to-run variation. Say so instead of implying stability.
- When repetitions exist, report all of them or their mean and spread, not the best one.

## 4. Choosing A Test

| Situation | Usual choice |
|---|---|
| Two independent groups, roughly normal | Welch's t-test |
| Two paired measurements | paired t-test; Wilcoxon signed-rank when not normal |
| Two independent groups, not normal or ordinal | Mann-Whitney U |
| Three or more groups | one-way ANOVA with a post-hoc test; Kruskal-Wallis when not normal |
| Two categorical variables | chi-square; Fisher's exact test with small counts |
| Two yes/no outcomes on the same items | McNemar's test |
| Relationship between two continuous variables | Pearson r, or Spearman rho when not linear or not normal |

Report the test, the statistic, the degrees of freedom where they apply, the exact p-value, and an effect size (Cohen's d, a difference with its interval, an odds ratio, r). A p-value alone is not a result.

Do not run a test the design cannot support. With one run per condition there is nothing to test; describe the difference and its resolution instead.

## 5. Multiple Comparisons And Selection

- Count the comparisons made. With several, correct for it (Holm or Bonferroni) or state that the comparisons are descriptive.
- Data used to choose a model, a setting or a threshold cannot also give an unbiased estimate of its performance. Keep a held-out set that plays no part in any choice and evaluate on it once.
- Do not tune on the test set, and do not use it to break ties.

## 6. Wording

- "Higher in this experiment" is a description. "Better" in general needs more than one setting, sample or dataset.
- Not significant does not mean no effect. Report the interval so the reader sees what sizes of effect remain possible.
- Name confounds: when two things changed together (dose and duration, sample size and measurement time), the result cannot be assigned to one of them.
- State what was not tested, and limit the conclusion to the conditions that were.

## 7. Final Checks For This Genre

1. Every reported statistic can be regenerated by the saved script.
2. n is stated for every number.
3. Every difference has a sign, a unit and something to judge its size against.
4. Claims of significance name the test and give the statistic and exact p-value.
5. The conclusion does not go beyond the tested conditions.
